story.name: Entry 71 | Breaking the Silence Through Play - Using Educational Games to Create Awareness

content.title: Entry 71 | Breaking the Silence Through Play - Using Educational Games to Create Awareness
content.author: Jenna Sara Khoja and Kiran Qasim Ali

content.text: This month, we discuss something essential yet often overlooked in education: girls' health and hygiene, with a particular focus on menstrual health. Silence and stigma still surround the topic in Pakistan's schools, where formal curricula rarely address it and many girls are left to navigate myths and misconceptions on their own. This article explores how game-based learning can serve as a culturally sensitive and engaging approach to break through barriers, dispel misinformation, and empower adolescent girls with accurate knowledge.
A Hidden Reality

This young girl's experience is not just an isolated case but a reflection of a broader and deeply ingrained issue affecting millions of adolescent girls across Pakistan. Menstruation is a normal, healthy, and natural biological process that all females inevitably experience. However, a 2017 survey conducted by UNICEF in Pakistan revealed that nearly half of females between the ages of 10 and 35 knew nothing about menstruation before their first period (Lihemo & Hafeez-Ur-Rehman, 2017). Among the estimated 22% of the school-going girls, who have begun menstruating, most lack access to the facilities necessary to manage their menstrual cycles hygienically (Bhatti & Boulard, 2018). Girls' health and hygiene, particularly menstrual health, is surrounded by silence and stigma, resulting in widespread ignorance and neglect of girls' health issues. Without proper knowledge, many adolescent girls struggle with basic hygiene, miss school due to unmanaged symptoms, endure preventable health problems, and fail to recognise signs of abnormalities. Addressing menstrual health in schools is therefore not an optional addition but an urgent educational and public health need.
The Current Curriculum Gap
Although menstrual health is central to adolescent well-being, it remains absent from Pakistan's formal curriculum. The draft
National Education Policy 2017

frames health education almost entirely within the scope of sport and physical training (Proff, Fatima, & Limón, 2023; Ministry of Federal Education and Professional Training, 2017). What is omitted from the curriculum is also omitted from legitimate classroom discourse. Teachers and students alike receive the signal that menstruation is not an educational concern, reinforcing silence and stigma. The absence of curricular attention shifts the responsibility for guidance almost entirely onto families, especially mothers and older sisters. These intergenerational exchanges reflect care, resilience, and cultural continuity, yet they benefit from being complemented by school-based education. Family knowledge has limits: it may not always draw on scientific evidence, leaving myths such as avoiding bathing, exercise, or certain foods unchallenged (Ali et al., 2006). It can also vary widely; while some girls receive clear and supportive guidance, others grow up with little or no information. The concern, therefore, is not the role of families -which remains vital - but the unevenness of what girls learn and the risk of misinformation when schools do not provide a consistent foundation.
Schools as Critical Sites

Integrating girls' health and hygiene into school education is essential not only for their physical, emotional, and psychosocial well-being but also for rethinking how sensitive topics are taught. A well-structured curriculum provides reliable, scientifically accurate knowledge that corrects harmful myths and misconceptions - the very beliefs that underpin unsafe practices. Yet the challenge is not merely curricular content but also pedagogy as teachers require strategies to facilitate open, respectful, and age-appropriate discussions on menstruation. Without such pedagogical support, even well-designed materials risk remaining underutilised or avoided due to discomfort. Effective classroom engagement can normalise conversations, reduce stigma, and create safe spaces where both girls and boys learn to view menstruation as a matter of health rather than shame. When girls are empowered with accurate knowledge and inclusive teaching practices, they are better prepared to make informed decisions, seek support when needed, and exercise agency over their health and personal development.
Play as a Pedagogical Response

When addressing culturally sensitive subjects such as menstrual health, conventional lecture-based methods are often ineffective. In many classrooms, direct instruction risks creating discomfort or resistance among students, teachers, and even parents. In such contexts, pedagogy matters as much as content: how knowledge is introduced can determine whether it is received, questioned, or ignored.

Game-based learning offers a distinctive pedagogical response. Unlike lectures, games create an indirect and less confrontational pathway into discussion. They allow learners to engage with difficult themes through scenarios, rules, and choices, rather than through direct personal disclosure. This playful structure reduces embarrassment, diffuses tension, and enables participation in a way that feels safer and more manageable. For teachers, games provide a structured yet flexible medium through which sensitive material can be introduced without triggering defensiveness.

From a psychological perspective, games also align with how young people process new and potentially uncomfortable information. They foster motivation by combining challenge with reward, and they encourage rehearsal of ideas through repeated interaction. Rather than simply hearing a statement that contradicts a cultural myth, students test and re-test their assumptions within the game space, correcting misconceptions in the process. This active engagement makes knowledge more memorable and more likely to influence behaviour than passive instruction.

Importantly, positioning games at the centre of pedagogy for topics such as menstruation does not mean exaggerating their impact. Games are not a panacea. But they are a particularly well-suited tool because they open up space for dialogue where silence and stigma would otherwise prevail. By embedding accurate information within familiar, interactive formats, they offer both teachers and learners a practical means to engage with an otherwise avoided subject.
Piloting Games with Teachers: Insights from Practice
In the AKU-IED workshop held in August, teacher educators, school nurses, and schoolteachers gathered to play a
Cycles and Climbs: A Menstruation Journey

, game designed around common misconceptions about the menstrual cycle. Each square presented a statement: misconceptions were represented by snakes that sent the player downward, while accurate knowledge was rewarded with a ladder. The familiar format immediately put participants at ease, allowing them to enter a sensitive conversation through play rather than formal instruction.
The dynamics of the game quickly drew participants into debate. When one teacher landed on a snake after agreeing with the statement
"Girls should not bathe during menstruation"

, her colleagues immediately questioned her response. A discussion followed, in which another participant shared her own experience of students missing school for several days because they believed bathing would worsen their condition. The group collectively worked through the evidence card, eventually reframing bathing as a hygienic practice that reduces infection risk. What might have been a defensive moment in another setting became a collaborative correction, with the game mechanics providing a neutral reason to revisit assumptions.
Another shift emerged when the board presented the claim that
"Girls should avoid physical activity while menstruating."

One participant hesitated, initially nodding in agreement. But a school nurse in the group, encouraged by the 'ladder' for rejecting the claim, explained how exercise had reduced cramps and improved attendance for her students. This example not only corrected the misconception but also prompted a wider discussion about how schools could create supportive environments for girls to continue sports during their cycle.
Even lighter moments carried pedagogical weight. When a player celebrated climbing a ladder after identifying the myth that
"eating certain foods increases bleeding"

, others laughed and admitted they had heard the same belief at home. The humour of the situation softened the stigma, giving participants permission to voice doubts and then collectively dismantle them. The laughter marked not dismissal but relief - a signal that discussing these topics in a classroom could be done without fear or shame.
These exchanges demonstrated that the pedagogical strength of the game lay in the
process

as much as the content. The snakes created teachable setbacks, requiring groups to pause, explain, and rethink, while the ladders validated accurate knowledge and rewarded progress. The pedagogical value of the game lay not in the transfer of facts alone but in the way it rehearsed dialogue. Teachers practised articulating responses to misconceptions, experimented with language they might use in classrooms, and observed how peers reframed sensitive issues without judgement. In doing so, they modelled the kind of respectful, open conversation that they would later need to facilitate with their own students.
From Workshop to Classrooms: Opportunities and Challenges
The workshop illustrated how a simple
Snakes and Ladders

game can help teachers address misconceptions and open conversations about menstruation. The next step is to consider what it would take to embed such approaches within classroom practice. We strongly believe that opportunities lie in the accessibility and adaptability of games. They provide a familiar structure that lowers hesitation, invite discussion in ways lectures often cannot, and can be tailored to address a range of sensitive topics beyond menstruation. Games also offer teachers a practical tool to create safe, structured spaces where myths can be surfaced and corrected through dialogue. However, the challenges must also be acknowledged. Teachers need preparation not only in how to facilitate game-based learning but also in how to handle sensitive discussions with care. Their own misconceptions may need to be clarified first. Time pressures within an already crowded curriculum can limit opportunities for sustained gameplay, and without formal recognition in curriculum frameworks, such efforts risk remaining occasional rather than systematic.

The implications are therefore twofold. First, professional development is crucial: teachers require training in both content and pedagogy if games are to be more than a novelty. Second, curriculum space must be secured so that menstrual health and related topics are not relegated to the margins but treated as integral to students' education. When these conditions are met, classroom games can move from being isolated interventions to becoming effective tools for normalising dialogue, challenging myths, and equipping students with reliable knowledge about their health.

body.quote: In the remote Kalash Valley of Chitral, nestled among the mountains of northern Pakistan, an 11-year-old girl stepped quietly into adolescence. She was younger than most of her peers when the changes began, yet like so many others, she faced them without guidance. In her community, menstruation was a subject cloaked in secrecy. No one had spoken to her about what to expect, and no one offered advice on how to manage it. Confused and frightened, she hid her symptoms from her family and friends. To cope, she tore scraps of old fabric into makeshift pads, constantly anxious that someone would notice. The physical pain she experienced forced her to miss school, but the greater burden was the silence: not knowing whom to ask, what was normal, or how to care for herself. What should have been a natural stage of growing up instead became a source of shame, absence, and quiet suffering.
